newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Privatization could spawn next LatAm debt crisis.
newsitem.headline: Privatization could spawn next LatAm debt crisis.

text.p: A next Latin American debt crisis may not stem from an exuberant petro-dollar lending binge as it did in the 1970s and 80s, but rather from something as innocuous as a road or bridge, World Bank economists predicted Thursday.

Government guarantees and subsidies masked as incentives to privately-funded projects across the region could mushroom into potentially huge liabilities that could dent sovereign credit ratings and even prompt default.
And that danger will be examined at a World Bank-sponsored conference in Cartagena this Thursday and Friday.

Free market reforms, growing credit markets, tight budgets and disenchantment with the performance of public services have brought a heady rush of private, billion dollar infrastructure projects to Latin America -- an estimated $7.8 billion in 1996, according to World Bank figures.
But with most Latin American macroeconomic and regulatory track records still shaky, many governments have had to lure prospective investors with grants, preferential tax treatment or guarantees.
"We want to draw attention to the issue," World Bank economist Mateen Thobani told Reuters in a telephone interview from Cartagena.
"It is not a serious problem now, but we think there could be significant chances of debt defaults say 15 years down the road ... and we want to point out ways to stop this happening."

Mexico has recently had to set aside 14 billion pesos to tackle toll road debts after lower than expected traffic left private sector operators -- such as Empresas ICA, Tribasa and Grupo Mexicano de Desarollo -- struggling for air.
"The operators took out huge loans, and banks were willing to lend as the roads were perceived as half government- sponsored projects which would be helped out if they went under," Thobani said.

With the trend towards privately-financed infrastructure seen growing in the region, the risk is that other troubled projects and subsequent bail-outs could damage sovereign credit ratings and in some cases even bring governments to their knees.

Various forms of insurance to the companies are one way forward, Thobani said. The public guarantees also represent a contingent liability that governments should reserve for. "Colombia has already started ... the only two other countries I know of are the U.S. and New Zealand," he added.
No numbers are available as to how large the potential liabilities are. "They may be small, or huge. At the moment, we just don't know," Thobani said.
But excessive use of guarantees also nixes the point of privatization: the private sector no longer needs to screen for white elephant projects, or run good projects efficiently.
"In effect, all these forms of support amount to some kind of subsidy ... If truly the government is short of money, that cannot work," noted a Bank discussion paper prepared for the conference.

In one example, the Venezuelan government recently backed off in the face of popular protest from raising tolls on the 10-mile (16 km) Caracas-La Guaira highway operated as a 30-year concession by Mexico's Empresas ICA. Instead, it exempted the operator from a 16.5 percent sales tax.
"Almost by definition, guarantees shift risks and costs from consumers to taxpayers," said the paper.
